intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that dystonia-25 (DYT25) is caused by heterozygous mutation in the GNAL gene on chromosome 18p.

paragraphs.text: Dystonia-25 is an autosomal dominant form of primary torsion dystonia with reduced penetrance. It mostly begins in adulthood, usually in the neck, and is mainly cervical dystonia. The age at onset varies widely, and in more than half of patients the dystonia spreads to other sites, especially the face and other cranial muscles. Speech can be affected. Arm involvement is uncommon (Fuchs et al., 2013).

paragraphs.text: Bressman et al. (1994) examined 53 people from 4 generations of a non-Jewish North American family with adult-onset idiopathic torsion dystonia. Seven family members were affected. Their mean age at onset was 28.4 years (range, 7 to 50 years). In 6 of the 7, the neck was affected first. All 7 developed cervical dystonia, and 5 had dysarthria or dysphonia.

paragraphs.text: Fuchs et al. (2013) reported 8 multiplex families with primary torsion dystonia and GNAL mutations. Complete clinical information was available for 28 people with definite dystonia, all of them Caucasian of mixed European ancestry. The average age at onset was 31.3 years (range, 7 to 54 years). Onset was in the neck in 82% of carriers, and 93% had neck involvement at the final examination. Most carriers developed dystonia at other sites, and only 46% still had focal dystonia at the last examination. Cranial involvement was present in 57% and speech involvement in 44%. No carrier had brachial onset, and only 32% eventually had arm involvement, which the authors noted distinguished this disorder from DYT6. Phenotypes varied within families carrying the same mutation. In 2 families, the proband had generalized dystonia that began in the legs, at ages 7 and 25 years. Other sites of onset in individual patients included the jaw, tongue, and larynx.

paragraphs.text: Fuchs et al. (2013) performed exome sequencing in 2 families with primary torsion dystonia. In family P, which had mixed Russian and Swiss Mennonite heritage, they found a heterozygous nonsense mutation in the GNAL gene (S293X) within a linkage region. The mutation was shared by the 3 affected family members who were sequenced and segregated with dystonia in the rest of the family. In family D1, they found a heterozygous missense mutation in GNAL (V137M) that segregated with the disease. V137M was not found in 572 control chromosomes, and neither mutation was found in about 3,500 European exomes in the NHLBI Exome Sequencing Project database.

paragraphs.text: Fuchs et al. (2013) then Sanger sequenced the GNAL coding region in 39 more multiplex families of mixed European origin with primary torsion dystonia who did not have DYT1 or DYT6 mutations. They found GNAL mutations in 6 of these families (19%). These were a nonsense mutation (R21X), 2 frameshift mutations (S95fsX110 and R198fsX210), a missense mutation (E155K), an in-frame deletion of 3 amino acids (P102_V104del), and a possible splice site mutation (c.274-5T-C). None of these variants was found in dbSNP135, in about 3,500 European exomes, or in 572 control chromosomes. In every family where DNA was available from more than one affected person, the mutation segregated with the disease. In a BRET assay of Galpha(olf) coupling to the D1 dopamine receptor, the S293X mutant did not support any D1R-driven response. The E155K and V137M mutants gave intermediate results, largely consistent with impaired binding to G-beta-gamma subunits. The authors concluded that the assay suggested loss of function.

agent.process_note: I read both papers in full: the Bressman et al. (1994) abstract and the Fuchs et al. (2013) full text, including Table 1. No reference data were supplied, so I took the gene location (chromosome 18p) from Fuchs et al. (2013) and left out the GNAL MIM number. Fuchs et al. (2013) say family D1 was reported before, but the citation was stripped from the text. D1's 7 affected members had onset ages averaging 28.4 years, ranging from 7 to 50, which matches the Bressman family, but the papers do not say outright that they are the same family, so I did not claim it. The supplementary pedigrees and tables were not available. I left out the mouse data because Fuchs et al. (2013) cite them only as background from other studies.
